newsitem.title: USA: Delta must improve service, fleet - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Delta must improve service, fleet - analysts.

text.p: Delta Air Lines Inc's plan to overhaul its transAtlantic and European networks will only succeed if the airline can quickly improve service and upgrade its fleet, analysts said.

Delta said Tuesday it would take a charge of about $60 million to revamp its European schedule and bolster its presence at New York's JFK International Airport. The moves were aimed at fixing problems dating back to its 1991 acquisition of Pan Am's European routes, analysts said.
Delta will also cut 600 to 800 employees in Frankfurt, Germany, as well as in St. Petersburg, Bucharest and Warsaw.
"Now that they've got the schedule and routes in shape, they need to improve the fleet and the product. But they recognize the urgency of this," said PaineWebber analyst Samuel Buttrick.
Delta's international business class service and amenities are among the worst in the industry, analysts said.
Delta said it will announce an overhaul of its transAtlantic premium class services within the next four or five weeks.
"That will give them an in-flight product that is consistent with their market presence. You don't want to be offering the most flights with the worst service," Buttrick said.

Delta also said it will make a "major decision" on aircraft purchases within the next 60 days. Delta is evaluating the Airbus Industrie 330, Boeing Co 777, or the Boeing 767-400 as possible replacements for its fleet of aging L-1011s.
Delta may also replace other aircraft orders. The airline declined to comment on the extent of a possible order.
Delta's plan to prune its international operations were "arguably" overdue, Buttrick said.

But the move will now help Delta protect its international market share from growing competition from mega-alliances such as Deutsche Lufthansa AG -UAL Corp's United Airlines, and the proposed British Airways Plc -AMR Corp's American Airlines deal, analysts said.
"It would have been better for them to do this earlier, but it's still a good environment to be doing it now," said Timothy Ross, an airline analyst with SBC Warburg Inc.
"It does improve their competitive position by deploying certain underperforming assets, yet without diluting their presence in Europe," Ross said.
Analyst said Delta was slow to revamp its international operations because the airline was struggling with its $1.2 billion purchase of Pan Am's international routes.
Delta first needed to absorb that purchase and study the route profitability. The airline also needed to secure strong European alliances, said Jeffrey Long, an analyst with J.P. Morgan Securities.

Delta defended its Pan Am purchase, saying the deal gave it a strong foothold in key European markets. The Pan Am acquisition, plus it alliances with nine European carriers, gave Delta new strength overseas, the company said.
Pan Am "was one of the most important strategic moves we have made. We didn't have control of the timing. But that accquisition is allowing us to make this move today," chairman Ronald Allen said.
"We now have the flexibility in place," Allen said. "It all goes back to the Pan Am acquistion."
Analysts see most of Delta's passenger revenue growth coming from its international operations.
Once Delta phases in the European restructuring, analysts expect the company to more aggressively expand service to India and South America. Delta also said it was pursuing alliances in China.
